Within this, too, certain idioms appear: binary formats typically use some form of TLV encoding, use different magics to signal different endiannesses, &c.

The tar format does not look like this, regardless of the variant. tar is fundamentally a block format, owing to its origins as a tape archival format8.

As a block format, a tar archive is comprised of one or more fixed-length blocks. There is no file-level header; instead, many of its blocks are headers, while other blocks contain actual member9 data:

In all flavors of tar, all blocks (including the header blocks) are always 512 bytes. Each header block declares metadata for the member that follows it. This includes important things like the size of the member and its filepath.

Member contents don't always fit cleanly into multiples of 512 bytes, so a tar that wants to encode a file member of N bytes will allocate ceil(N / 512) blocks and pad out the remainder of the last block. This doesn't affect extraction, since the reader knows (via the header block) exactly how many bytes out of the allocated space are actual file content.

Conventionally, the padding or "holes" in a tar archive are filled with NUL bytes. However, nothing stops a tar producer from filling them with uninitialized memory, or lines from the Bee Movie, or anything else. A recurring theme with tar (of all flavors) is that it has no opinions about what goes in the holes of the format. This malleability makes it very prone to parser differentials, since it gives the attacker ample space to place surprising data.

tar's block design also makes it relatively space-inefficient10 by modern standards. For example, a 513-byte file occupies an absolute minimum of 1,536 bytes when encoded as a tar member: one 512-byte block for the header, and two blocks for the content (one of which has only 1 "real" byte, followed by 511 bytes of padding). Similarly, a tar archive containing 1000 one-byte files requires a minimum of 1025 KiB of encoding (1 MiB for the headers and contents, and then 1 KiB for the trailing zero blocks).

tar problems #

So far, this all sounds pretty sane. It's not a "normal" file format by modern standards, but there's a simple state machine one could write to formalize a parse for the tar example above:

Unfortunately, it's not that simple. The state machine above is accurate for a V7 tar, but not for anything else in the tar format family.

To understand why, we have to remember V7 tar's limitations. All of those limitations come down to the C structure that represents a V7 member header, which we've annotated here:

struct v7_header {
    // The member's path. Observe that this can be no more than 100 bytes;
    // NUL termination isn't required, since it's a fixed-size field.
	char name[100];

    // The member's mode, as an octal string.
    // Note that only the first 4 octal digits (12 bits) have well-defined semantics in pax.
	char mode[8];

    // The member's owner's UID and GID, as octal strings.
	char uid[8];
	char gid[8];

    // The size of the member, as an octal string.
    // V7 treats this as NUL-terminated, so the largest
    // interoperable value in it is `77777777777\0`.
	char size[12];

    // The member's mtime, as an octal string.
	char mtime[12];

    // A checksum for the member header itself.
	char chksum[8];

    // '\0' for a regular file, '1' for a hard link,
    // and '2' for a symbolic link.
	char linkflag;

    // When `linkflag` is '1' or '2', this is the link's destination.
    // Like `name` this is limited to 100 bytes.
	char linkname[100];

    // 255 bytes of the header are unused.
	char pad[255];
};

Three big limitations stand out, and each member of the tar family tries to solve them in various different ways:

  1. Member and link names cannot be longer than 100 bytes;
  2. Members cannot be larger than 0o77777777777 bytes, i.e. one byte short of 8 GiB;
  3. Only regular files and links are defined; there are no directory or other member types11.

Let's see how each family works around these.

UStar and pax #

UStar's half-solution is to preserve the existing physical header block, while impressing some of its fields and padding into new roles.

This is the UStar header:

struct ustar_header {
    // Unchanged.
	char name[100];
	char mode[8];
	char uid[8];
	char gid[8];
	char size[12];
	char mtime[12];
	char checksum[8];

    // `linkflag` is now `typeflag`, and encodes, inter alia,
    // '5' for a directory.
	char typeflag[1];

    // Unchanged.
	char linkname[100];

    // `"ustar\0"`
	char magic[6];

    // `"00"`
	char version[2];

    // The user and group names for the member.
	char uname[32];
	char gname[32];

    // For chardev/blockdev members, the device's major and minor numbers.
	char devmajor[8];
	char devminor[8];

    // If nonempty, a prefix to prepend to `name` (joined by a `/`).
	char prefix[155];

    // 12 remaining bytes of the header are unused.
	char pad[12];
};

This partially lifts the member name restriction (by raising it to 255 bytes), but retains the file size and linkname limitations.

pax fixes these remaining limitations by doing away with the single-block metadata design. Instead, pax has extensions that rely on two new UStar typeflags:

  • Typeflag 'x' indicates a local extended header block.
  • Typeflag 'g' indicates a global extended header block.

In both cases, an extended header block indicates its member's "size." But that size isn't for a file: instead, it's for the extension data itself.

So, what's in the extension data? pax calls it an extended header, and it's an entirely different encoding format. An extended header contains one or more pax "records," and each record is a string that looks like this:

<length> <keyword>=<value>\n

where:

  • <length> is the byte-length of the record itself, including <length> itself12;
  • <keyword> is a keyword that sets or overrides some pax parsing state;
  • <value> is the value to apply to <keyword>.

In the example above, this means that the subsequent member's size is 8000 bytes, even if the member's own header records a different size.

GNU tar #

GNU tar takes a very different approach. First, here's the GNU tar header:

struct gnu_header {
    // Unchanged from UStar.
	char name[100];
	char mode[8];

    // Same layout as UStar, but potentially base-256.
	char uid[8];
	char gid[8];
	char size[12];
	char mtime[12];
	char checksum[8];

    // Same layout as UStar, but additional typeflags.
	char typeflag[1];

    // Unchanged.
	char linkname[100];

    // `"ustar "`
	char magic[6];

    // `" \0"`
	char version[2];

    // Unchanged from UStar.
	char uname[32];
	char gname[32];
	char devmajor[8];
	char devminor[8];

    // GNU extensions.
	char atime[12];
	char ctime[12];
	char offset[12];
	char longnames[4];
	char unused[1];
	struct {
		char offset[12];
		char numbytes[12];
	} sparse[4];
	char isextended[1];
	char realsize[12];

    // 17 remaining bytes of the header are unused.
	char pad[17];

Observe that, unlike the UStar format, there is no char prefix[155] field. Furthermore, instead of pax extended headers with a fully general keyword/value format, GNU tar does two things:

  • It goes way harder than UStar on trying to re-use the existing 512-byte V7 member header. In particular, GNU tar adds its own base-256 encoding: if the first byte in a numeric field has its high bit set, then the remaining octets in that field are binary, rather than tar's normal octal form. This effectively expands the per-byte entropy in numeric fields from 3 bits to 8 bits. For a char size[12], that makes the effective size limit 2**8014 or one yobibyte.
  • Instead of general x and g extended headers, GNU tar introduces a bunch of specialized typeflags for its own extensions. Many of these are not relevant to the post, or even to modern tar archives at all. But two are: The L typeflag identifies the next sequence of content blocks as containing a filename. The K typeflag identifies the next sequence of content blocks as containing a link name. These two typeflags effectively fill the role of the pax path and linkpath records, respectively.

State machine turducken #

Now that we understand very roughly how the various tar family formats look and work, let's see what tar-codec has to do to parse them safely and efficiently.

First we'll revisit the state machine. Our nice and simple V7 state machine now understands the different pax and GNU states, and has become this monstrosity:

(Note that the error transitions in this state machine are dramatically simplified: in practice, any I/O or validation failure at any point also results in a Failed state.)

What in the world happened? A few different things:

  • Our state machine begins with a "classification" stage, which effectively locks the remainder of the parse to a single family (either UStar/pax or GNU16) based on the identity (magic and version) of the first block. This is done for differential reduction reasons: while researching tar-codec's design, we realized that many other widely used tar parsers attempt to merge states across various tar families, with inconsistent results. For example, with some tar parsers, it's possible to stack headers like so: This has unclear semantics: GNU tar expects an L or K to apply to the next "file" member, but the next physical member in the stream is a pax local extension that also wants to modify the next "file" member. In practice we've seen other parsers do all kinds of things in this state, including attempting to merge the extensions, honoring one over the other(s), attempting to apply the L state to x instead of the file member, and so forth. Each of these is a potentially exploitable differential! Instead, tar-codec will reject a tar archive if its individual headers don't agree about what family of tar it is. Real-world tar encoders don't mix tar families (there's no good reason to), so this doesn't pose a significant breakage risk.
  • The GNU part of the state machine is slightly more strict than the GNU documentation implies: the GNU documentation allows stacking of L/K extensions, including multiple of the same kind, in any order. tar-codec tightens that to allowing L and K in any order, but only one of each per underlying member.
  • The UStar/pax part of the state machine models local and global extended headers rigidly. There's a significant amount of complexity beneath this: pax allows x and g anywhere in the tar stream. For example, this is a perfectly valid extension sequence in pax: This brings us to one of the most painful parts of pax that we glossed over before: extended headers don't shadow each other fully, they compose depending on what state the "stack" of effective pax records is in. The state of any given pax record can be: Undeclared: no effective pax record exists anywhere in the current stack of local and global extensions, which means that the member's own UStar header's state takes precedence. Active: there's an effective pax record in the stack, and it has a value. Tombstoned: there's an effective pax record in the stack, but it has no value (for example, 8 path=\n instead of 12 path=abc\n). You would think that this would be the same as the Undeclared state, but it's not! pax considers this record explicitly deleted, and prescribes: If the <value> field is zero length, it shall delete any header block field, previously entered extended header value, or global extended header value of the same name. This has fascinating consequences for the state machine, because it means that an effective-but-deleted path record means...a file with no path? How are you supposed to extract that17? Needless to say, tar-codec tries to follow this faithfully. In particular, it attempts to be diligent about rejecting logically-consistent-but-nonsense states that fall out of pax's strange record state machine, including empty paths and global extended headers that try to declare size and other key states for all members.

From parsing to extraction #

One of the early design choices we made with tar-codec was to isolate the implementation into a few layers. From lowest to highest:

  • The tar-framing crate is responsible for taking a stream of blocks and turning it into a stream of frames. This happens in two refinement stages: The stream or "physical" API honors the big state machine above and yields each block in a given state, one block at a time. The "logical" API consumes the blocks produced by the "physical" API, and yields them as a stream of assembled members. Each assembled member is essentially its "header" (which is the physical header, merged with any effective extension state that affected the physical framing), a separate extension state for non-framing extensions (such as GNU L and K), and a readable payload for the member's actual contents.
  • The tar-codec crate takes the "logical" API from tar-framing and turns it into something that can be extracted in memory or onto disk.

Extracting an archive (of any format) onto disk is its own can of worms, with its own differential risks18. Another one of our early observations is that every archive implementation tends to have its own extract-to-disk implementation, with its own edge cases.

We built archive-trait to address that. archive-trait exposes Archive and ArchiveBuilder traits (along with associated types and machinery) that allow any format to expose uniform APIs for reading and creating archives. We then built archive-trait's own filesystem extraction on top of cap-std, giving us the ability to "anchor" extraction into a single directory and avoid a large class of link and path traversal footguns.

Lessons learned #

  • Writing a differential-resistant tar parser is surprisingly hard, given how ubiquitous tar files of all flavors are, and how simple the original (V7) format is. This post has only scratched the surface in terms of complexity. To recap: Each tar family has its own state machine, which is not always clearly laid out in that family's documentation or reference implementation. It is imperative that these state machines do not mix, but real-world tar parsers regularly allow them to. Each tar family has its own, non-trivial rules for determining the precedence of state (pathname, linkname, and size) attached to archive members. Some of this state affects the framing of the parser itself, meaning that faithfully handling e.g. pax archives means handling size and similar records up-front, rather than trying to abstract the parse across individual 512-byte header blocks. Separately, there were numerous places where we had to compromise on strict pax conformance because of observed behavior from other implementations: The pax spec is explicit that pax record values must be UTF-8. However, both GNU tar and star historically emitted some vendor-specific records19 as raw binary. See this bug-tar thread for more context. UStar and pax are explicit that uname and gname should be NUL-terminated in the UStar header, meaning that each can be at most 31 bytes long. However, CPython's tarfile (and probably others) will happily fill either to 32 bytes, only overflowing to the pax record at 33 bytes or more. See CPython#159322 for more context. More generally, tar implementations will frequently leave mode, uid, gid, and mtime as all NUL, rather than zeroed or similar. This doesn't pose a framing/parser synchronization risk, so tar-codec tracks them as "missing" rather than assigning an arbitrary default value. Finally, in the process of designing and implementing tar-codec, we found many parser differential primitives that cause various tar implementations to behave very differently on identical inputs. Some of these are currently being disclosed as security vulnerabilities. However, some of the general classes we saw: pax/GNU state machine confusion, as mentioned above. In particular, some tar implementations can be fooled into applying a pax extension's states to a GNU extension (or vice versa) instead of to the subsequent member, often resulting in full desynchronization and different extraction results. Mis-handling of pax extension precedence, in particular both global (g) extended headers and record "tombstoning." For example, some implementations will accept a g header with size=1234 but ignore it, despite pax saying clearly that such a size record overrides any UStar size fields. This also typically results in a full desynchronization primitive. Mis-handling of pax record parsing. For example, some implementations will ignore the <length> prefix and instead assume that pax records can be safely split on \n. This is not true, since the <value> of a pax record can contain a verbatim \n. As you may have guessed, this also typically results in a full desynchronization primitive. More generally, we found a great deal of variety in how lax various tar implementations are when it comes to parsing integer fields: many use their language's native "integer from string" API, which can behave surprisingly in the presence of different (non-Western Arabic) numeral forms, leading and trailing whitespace, and so forth. These small variations can percolate into two different implementations parsing the same size field as different integers, once again resulting in desynchronization.
  • Decode and encode performance was not the hard part: we found a lot of low-hanging fruit while optimizing both, including optimizing tar's checksum generation and calculating pax record length prefixes. We also picked up significant performance gains by ensuring that tar-codec reuses allocations and batches/buffers its work wherever possible (and where doing so does not weaken the API's internal consistency or cancellation correctness in an async setting).
  • Conversely, performant secure extraction is somewhat hard: directory capability tracking (of the kind that cap-std does) adds measurable overhead to many of our filesystem operations, particularly when extracting on hosts that lack openat2(2) or an equivalent system call20. This negatively impacts extraction on macOS in particular.

All in all, tar-codec's design rests on well-worn principles for secure parser design: we are conservative rather than liberal in what we accept, and we enforce correctness by construction through increasingly constrictive layers (from member framing to streaming to extraction). These design choices have made us confident that tar-codec is more resistant to differentials (by correctly rejecting them) than other tar implementations.

The fractured and under-specified nature of tar makes it impossible for us to say that we are entirely devoid of differentials, or that new differentials won't be discovered in the future. However, we believe that tar-codec's primitives are the correct ones if and when those contingencies occur.

Looking forwards #

This is not the end of our work, on several levels:

  • While tar-codec is essentially feature-complete for our own purposes (within uv), we're interested in making sure that it also solves problems that the larger Open Source community has around secure and performant tar parsing. To that end, we'll be looking at supporting other, more niche aspects of the various tar families (like sparse files, and more control over vendor-specific pax records) as the need arises. Separately, we'll be working with others in the community on improving the correctness of other tar implementations. In particular, we see Harmen Stoppels's nascent tar-minefield project as a promising way to test and re-align other implementations with stricter, more differential-resistant interpretations of the tar family formats.
  • Separately, as you may have guessed from our decision to build a generic archive-trait library: tar is not the only format we're thinking about here! We're also actively looking into replacing uv's ZIP parsing, for similar reasons. We hope to share our lessons from that work soon, along with material benefits to uv itself.
